Consult Summary:
- 26-year-old male with history of asthma and recent upper respiratory tract infection presenting with 3-hour history of chest tightness, mild shortness of breath, wheeze, and cough, after running out of inhalers for one week.

History:
- Presenting complaint: Chest tightness for 3 hours.
- Timeline:
  - Symptoms began 3 hours prior to consult.
  - Cough and cold symptoms started last week, improved somewhat, but cough persisted.
  - Chest tightness, wheeze, and mild shortness of breath developed today.
- Associated symptoms: 
  - Wheeze, mild shortness of breath (not at rest), cough (non-productive), feels like cannot get a full breath.
  - Previously had sore throat and runny nose last week; now less pronounced.
  - Cough is a little worse at night but generally consistent.
- Recent exacerbating factors: 
  - Ran out of both asthma inhalers (Clenil and Salbutamol) one week ago while away at university; has not used them in the past week.
- Relieving factors: None noted.
- No chest pain (tightness only).
- Systems review:
  - No cough productive of sputum.
  - No shortness of breath at rest, only on exertion (e.g., when climbing stairs).
  - No reported fever, ear pain, or other symptoms at this time.
  - No known drug allergies; environmental allergies to dust and history of hayfever.

Past Medical History:
- Asthma (childhood onset), with history of severe exacerbation requiring hospitalization and intubation at age 16–17.
- Hayfever.
- Allergies: Dust, hayfever; no medication allergies.
- Past history of eczema (childhood) and milk protein allergy (childhood).
- Usual medications:
  - Ventolin (Salbutamol) inhaler (“dose/route/frequency not documented”; did not use for past week, as ran out).
  - Clenil Modulite inhaler (“dose/route/frequency not documented”; did not use for past week, as ran out).

Social History:
- Was away at university last week.
- No details regarding smoking, alcohol, or other substance use.
- No relevant financial or lifestyle factors mentioned.
- Lives independently; implied university student.

Family History:
- Mother: Eczema.
- Father: Asthma.

Physical Examination:
- No documented examination or vital signs.

Investigations:
- No investigations, imaging, or test results documented.
- Patient does not have access to a peak flow meter.

Assessment & Plan:
- Issue 1: Asthma exacerbation likely triggered by recent viral URTI and non-adherence due to running out of inhalers.
  - Prescriptions to be provided for Ventolin (Salbutamol) inhaler and Clenil Modulite inhaler.
  - Prescribe a 5-day course of oral steroids (specific drug/dose not documented; instruction: two tablets in the morning).
  - Prescribe a spacer device and provide instructions for use.
  - Advise use of Clenil Modulite regularly (morning), with Ventolin to be used as needed for wheeze.
  - Advise seeking urgent medical attention if requiring more frequent Ventolin (i.e., more than every three hours), experiencing worsening shortness of breath, chest pain/tightness, light-headedness, or other concerning symptoms.
  - Advise rest and consider time off work; self-certification for up to 7 days recommended.
- Issue 2: Allergic history/hayfever.
  - No acute management discussed.
- Issue 3: None identified.

General plan items:
- Encourage review of steroid information and side effects.
- Safety net: Escalate to medical care if any deterioration.
- No acute need for hospital assessment currently, as no shortness of breath at rest or severe symptoms.

Quality checks (document_quality):

●	Missing but clinically expected elements:
  - No vital signs or physical examination findings documented.
  - No details on medication doses, frequencies, or routes.
  - No current peak flow measurement.
  - No detailed review of other systems, smoking/alcohol status, or living arrangements.
  - No allergies listed in summarized form (but documented verbally—environmental only).
●	Internal conflicts:
  - None detected.
●	Transcript quality:
  - Minor audio/connection interruptions, but clinical information clear. No major omissions.
